items.title: Add Up Every Fear and You Die Daily | Geeta Ramanujam, Storyteller
items.description:
Fear of losing status, of losing someone, of losing the groceries you buy every week. Add each one up, says Geeta Ramanujam, and you're dying a thousand times every day. She tells me about her three encounters with death: a flight that burst into flames minutes after landing, and a near-drowning off a quiet island in Thailand. Only after those, she says, did she become a storyteller.

items.title: "How Do You Do Your Pricing?" Nobody Has a Straight Answer | Lowell Mora, Fractional CFO
items.description:
First question Lowell Mora asks clients: how do you do your pricing? He almost never gets a straight answer — cost-plus, market, "both," costs that aren't fully loaded. Then the SaaS twist: unlimited customers, habit pricing like Netflix at $9.99, and why incumbents (Zoom/Teams) win even when a better product is cheaper — switching friction. Debate still open: underprice to enter, then raise — or leave money on the table forever?

items.title: Nothing Happens Until You Sell — Then Cash Kills You | Lowell Mora, Fractional CFO
items.description:
Bootstrap trap: the founder does sales because they're "free" — but a great engineer isn't always the person who should sell. Lowell Mora: nothing happens until you sell something; self-awareness means don't do what someone else can do better. Then the kill shot: businesses rarely die because they can't be profitable — they die because they run out of cash. Do the 13-week cashflow. I push back on the cost of hiring experts when every dollar hurts; we leave that debate open.

items.title: Street Dogs, Sacrifice, and What Nepal's Students Chose | Dr. Julie Palais, Animal-Law Advocate
items.description:
Julie Palais on the SAVE Nepal / CALS Global Ambassador work with law students in Kathmandu: four self-chosen research topics — street dogs, wildlife poaching, working animals, and animal sacrifice. The sacrifice paper went to Gadimai; the mayor's pushback was economic. Julie's own Nepal door: trekking, then Kukur Tihar — dogs celebrated one day, "back to the usual" the next — and the true story that became her children's book about a dog scalded with boiling water.
